raw_response:
I'm 58, been farming these same 6 mu in Quzhou for 40 years. Wheat then maize, that's the only way I know. My husband is doing construction work in Handan this year, so day-to-day it's mostly me on the farm, but he'll come back for the busy spells — wheat harvest and maize planting, when you need every hand and the window is tight.

I finished middle school, so I can read the numbers on the fertilizer bags and I listen when the extension agent comes by, but honestly, 40 years on this same soil teaches you more than any textbook. My neighbor Old Wang across the lane has been trying some fancy new wheat variety, but I'm sticking with the improved seed I've used for three years now. It gives me a steady 800 jin per mu — about 400 kg — and the seed costs me 35 yuan per mu. I buy fresh seed every couple of years to keep the vigor up; saved seed gets weak.

Money is tight. My husband's wages help, but we still watch every yuan. The extension fellow says I should put 15 kg of nitrogen on each mu of wheat, but fertilizer prices went up again this spring. I'm planning about 12–13 kg per mu — I spread compound fertilizer as base before sowing, around 50 kg per mu, and then if the wheat looks yellow at jointing in March, I topdress with urea. Twelve kg is a bit below what the book says, but my soil is decent and I've managed fine with this rate. Last year I tried to save money and only did 10 kg, and the yield dropped to 350 kg — that hurt. So this year I'll stick to 12–13 kg. Better to waste a little than risk a bad year.

For water, wheat is thirsty. I'll irrigate three times: once after sowing if October stays dry, once at jointing, and once at grain filling. Pumping from the well runs on electricity, about 20 yuan per mu each time, so wheat irrigation alone will cost me nearly 400 yuan. It stings, but you cannot skip jointing — that's when the grain heads set. For maize, once at the big trumpet stage is usually enough, maybe twice if August turns dry like last year. I'll budget for one time to be safe, another 120 yuan.

Maize goes in the ground right after wheat comes off — usually within three or four days. No time to plow. I hire a machine to no-till plant straight into the wheat stubble; costs 50 yuan per mu but saves me a week I don't have. I buy hybrid maize seed every year — 3.5 kg per mu at 50 yuan — because hybrid seed won't breed true. All the maize fertilizer goes in the furrow at planting: about 10 kg nitrogen and some phosphorus. I don't topdress maize; by the time I notice it needs more, it's too late and I don't have the labor anyway.

For chemicals, both crops get herbicide. Wheat might need a fungicide spray in April if I see rust — I had to spray once two years ago. Maize always needs watching for borers, especially with these warmer summers. I budget about 50–60 yuan per mu for pesticides on each crop.

Labor is mostly family. I figure about 14 days of my own work on wheat through the year — sowing, spreading fertilizer, moving pipes at night for irrigation, spraying, helping with harvest. Maize takes about 10 family days. I hire three days for wheat season and two for maize, mostly for machine work and when I need an extra pair of hands.

I expect about 400 kg per mu for wheat and 420 kg per mu for maize if the weather is normal. Total input costs — seed, fertilizer, water, chemicals, hired help, and machine hire — will run to about 3,200 yuan this year. That's a lot of cash to put out upfront, but we need the grain for our own table and the surplus to sell.
